foundations.title: Professional Foundations — California
foundations.action: Confirm licence or registration status, practice setting and required supervision.
foundations.record: Explain the practitioner’s role, confidentiality limits and the purpose of the service. Identify any separate statutory designation needed for assessment, reporting or detention work. Use supervision and continuing education to address competence, bias and the person’s feedback. BBS investigates relevant professional complaints; county services, benefit agencies and courts address other decisions. Explain which route can address the person’s concern rather than presenting professional discipline as a service appeal.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — California
care-support.action: Apply through the appropriate county and identify the current eligibility and health-certification requirements.
care-support.record: Describe functional needs, actual assistance required and the home environment during assessment. Check the authorised tasks, hours, notice and how a provider will be arranged. Track the hearing or review route and any request concerning continued benefits while a decision is challenged. CDSS State Hearings handles relevant disputes, including IHSS decisions. Read the notice for the applicable deadline and any earlier action needed to seek continued assistance. A provider complaint does not automatically preserve a benefit-hearing deadline.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — California
mca.action: Identify the specific healthcare, personal or financial decision and support the person’s participation.
mca.record: Check the relevant capacity standard and evidence rather than relying on diagnosis alone. Read the advance directive, appointment or court order and verify scope and operation. Use the applicable surrogate or court route if authority is missing or disputed. California Courts explains advance planning and conservatorship routes. A clinical consent dispute and a conservatorship petition have different procedures. Seek the relevant legal or clinical advice and preserve the person’s wishes and participation.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — California
dols.action: Identify the actual restriction, setting and the legal measure relied on.
dols.record: Read the hold, court order or specific restraint authority and check its scope and expiry. Distinguish the person’s detention status from medication consent and other healthcare decisions. Arrange patients’ rights support, the appropriate hearing or court route and a plan to reduce restrictions. County patients’ rights advocates and legal representatives help with applicable detention and treatment rights. Certification review and medication-capacity hearings address different questions. Explain the route relevant to the person’s objection rather than describing every challenge as the same appeal.

mha.title: Mental Health — California
mha.action: Identify the authorised person, proposed route and evidence for the current statutory criteria.
mha.record: Consider voluntary crisis support and whether the person can be served without detention. Check the start time, required assessment, notices and any further certification or court process. Keep detention and treatment-consent safeguards separate, including medication-capacity procedures where applicable. Explain access to the patients’ rights advocate, legal representation and the relevant hearing or court review. Additional detention is not automatic when an initial period ends. A broad social problem or lack of housing should not be substituted for the required statutory analysis.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — California
safeguarding.action: Identify the person’s statutory category, your reporting role, the alleged harm and the setting.
safeguarding.record: Make the required report through the correct APS, law-enforcement, ombudsman or other specified route. Check the applicable telephone and written or electronic follow-up deadlines; do not assume one rule covers every institution. Arrange immediate safety, consent-sensitive support and follow-up while preserving the adult’s account. A mandated report and the adult’s consent to ongoing services are different matters. Reporting does not itself appoint a conservator or authorise forced placement. Explain the relevant APS, regulatory, police or court process and available advocacy.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — California
children.action: Identify your mandated-reporter role and the facts supporting knowledge or reasonable suspicion.
children.record: Make the required report to an authorised receiving agency and address immediate danger. Complete the follow-up within the applicable time and record what was reported. Coordinate support and assess any dependency-court or Indian Child Welfare Act requirements where relevant. Explain confidentiality limits and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. A mandated report does not itself establish the legal grounds for removal or a court finding. Preserve the distinction between suspicion, investigation and adjudication.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — California
rights.action: Identify the organisation, service and applicable state and federal rights or privacy duties.
rights.record: Arrange disability access, interpretation and culturally responsive participation. Check the legal basis for disclosure and whether specially protected records or proceedings are involved. Explain access, correction, complaints and any applicable patient-rights or legal review route. HHS Office for Civil Rights handles covered HIPAA and Part 2 complaints; California and professional complaint routes address other matters. A subpoena, a court order and a routine agency request need distinct analysis. Seek appropriate advice rather than automatically releasing a complete file.

sources.title: California Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: The California Board of Behavioral Sciences (BBS) regulates Licensed Clinical Social Workers (LCSWs) and Associate Clinical Social Workers (ASWs). Licensure, associate registration, supervision and employer duties must be distinguished. Use the current BBS statutes, regulations and guidance for the practice setting.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: An ASW is not an independently licensed LCSW. A supervisor must meet the relevant requirements, and an employment title does not confer county-designated mental-health detention authority. NASW ethical material may inform practice but does not replace California licensing law.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Confirm licence or registration status, practice setting and required supervision. Explain the practitioner’s role, confidentiality limits and the purpose of the service. Identify any separate statutory designation needed for assessment, reporting or detention work. Use supervision and continuing education to address competence, bias and the person’s feedback.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: BBS investigates relevant professional complaints; county services, benefit agencies and courts address other decisions. Explain which route can address the person’s concern rather than presenting professional discipline as a service appeal.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Equating a degree, associate registration and independent clinical licensure.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) provides assessed in-home assistance to eligible aged, blind or disabled people. County assessment, authorised tasks and hours, financial or programme eligibility and actual provider arrangements are separate decisions. Medi-Cal services, regional-centre support and housing assistance have other rules.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: An IHSS Notice of Action explains the county decision and hearing rights. A disagreement about authorised hours is different from a problem recruiting a worker or a complaint about missed visits. Identify the disputed decision and the evidence relevant to it.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Apply through the appropriate county and identify the current eligibility and health-certification requirements. Describe functional needs, actual assistance required and the home environment during assessment. Check the authorised tasks, hours, notice and how a provider will be arranged. Track the hearing or review route and any request concerning continued benefits while a decision is challenged.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: CDSS State Hearings handles relevant disputes, including IHSS decisions. Read the notice for the applicable deadline and any earlier action needed to seek continued assistance. A provider complaint does not automatically preserve a benefit-hearing deadline.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating worker availability as proof that the assessed need has disappeared.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: California’s Probate Code provides decision-specific capacity and healthcare decision-making provisions, including advance healthcare directives, agents and surrogate arrangements. Probate conservatorship and Lanterman-Petris-Short (LPS) conservatorship are different processes; neither should be described simply as a family member taking over all decisions.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Read the directive, power or court order and identify the exact authority. Financial power does not automatically include healthcare. Where no existing authorised decision-maker is available, use the applicable Probate Code surrogate process with the responsible healthcare provider rather than assuming an informal next-of-kin hierarchy.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the specific healthcare, personal or financial decision and support the person’s participation. Check the relevant capacity standard and evidence rather than relying on diagnosis alone. Read the advance directive, appointment or court order and verify scope and operation. Use the applicable surrogate or court route if authority is missing or disputed.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: California Courts explains advance planning and conservatorship routes. A clinical consent dispute and a conservatorship petition have different procedures. Seek the relevant legal or clinical advice and preserve the person’s wishes and participation.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming financial authority, next-of-kin status or a conservatorship label answers every consent question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: The LPS framework provides particular mental-health detention and conservatorship routes. Probate conservatorship, healthcare consent and facility restraint rules are separate. An admission agreement or conservator’s general status does not explain every locked-door measure, restraint or treatment.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: A section 5150 hold is a time-limited assessment and crisis-intervention route, not an automatic order to keep someone for the whole maximum period or to impose every proposed treatment. Continuing detention requires the applicable further authority and safeguards.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the actual restriction, setting and the legal measure relied on. Read the hold, court order or specific restraint authority and check its scope and expiry. Distinguish the person’s detention status from medication consent and other healthcare decisions. Arrange patients’ rights support, the appropriate hearing or court route and a plan to reduce restrictions.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: County patients’ rights advocates and legal representatives help with applicable detention and treatment rights. Certification review and medication-capacity hearings address different questions. Explain the route relevant to the person’s objection rather than describing every challenge as the same appeal.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating detention, medication capacity and restraint authorisation as a single decision.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: The Lanterman-Petris-Short framework in the Welfare and Institutions Code includes section 5150 assessment and crisis intervention, subsequent certification routes and conservatorship. Section 5150 permits specified authorised persons to act on probable cause under the statutory conditions, for up to 72 hours. It is not a power held by every social worker.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: SB 43 expanded the grave-disability definition to include specified circumstances involving severe substance use disorder and inability to meet needs including personal safety or necessary medical care. Counties could defer implementation only until January 2026. Use the current section 5008 wording and criteria rather than an older food-clothing-shelter-only summary.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the authorised person, proposed route and evidence for the current statutory criteria. Consider voluntary crisis support and whether the person can be served without detention. Check the start time, required assessment, notices and any further certification or court process. Keep detention and treatment-consent safeguards separate, including medication-capacity procedures where applicable.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain access to the patients’ rights advocate, legal representation and the relevant hearing or court review. Additional detention is not automatic when an initial period ends. A broad social problem or lack of housing should not be substituted for the required statutory analysis.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using a superseded grave-disability definition or assuming all social workers can initiate a hold.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: California’s Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act includes mandated-reporting duties. Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630 addresses covered reporters and circumstances. County APS service eligibility and the statutory definitions used for reporting should be checked separately; an agency’s service age range should not be substituted for the legal definition.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Community, long-term-care, state-hospital and other institutional concerns can have different reporting recipients and timing rules. CDSS publishes general reporting guidance, but the actual setting and allegation determine which statutory provisions apply.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the person’s statutory category, your reporting role, the alleged harm and the setting. Make the required report through the correct APS, law-enforcement, ombudsman or other specified route. Check the applicable telephone and written or electronic follow-up deadlines; do not assume one rule covers every institution. Arrange immediate safety, consent-sensitive support and follow-up while preserving the adult’s account.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A mandated report and the adult’s consent to ongoing services are different matters. Reporting does not itself appoint a conservator or authorise forced placement. Explain the relevant APS, regulatory, police or court process and available advocacy.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Confusing APS service eligibility with statutory reporting definitions or treating an internal report as sufficient.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: The Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act (CANRA) specifies mandated reporters, reportable concerns and recipients. Penal Code section 11166 requires a covered reporter acting professionally or within employment to report knowledge or reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect. Certainty or medical proof is not required.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The ordinary procedure requires an initial telephone report immediately or as soon as practicably possible and a written follow-up within 36 hours. Reporting to a supervisor is not a substitute. Use the current statutory recipient and procedure, including any applicable special circumstances.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify your mandated-reporter role and the facts supporting knowledge or reasonable suspicion. Make the required report to an authorised receiving agency and address immediate danger. Complete the follow-up within the applicable time and record what was reported. Coordinate support and assess any dependency-court or Indian Child Welfare Act requirements where relevant.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain confidentiality limits and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. A mandated report does not itself establish the legal grounds for removal or a court finding. Preserve the distinction between suspicion, investigation and adjudication.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Waiting for certainty or a manager’s permission before making a required CANRA report.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in California practice guide?
cards.answer: Federal disability and civil-rights requirements and California protections apply according to the service and decision. For confidentiality, distinguish HIPAA-covered entities, California’s Confidentiality of Medical Information Act and other applicable state rules. A social-work record is not automatically governed by HIPAA solely because it contains sensitive information.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Certain substance-use-disorder records have additional protection under 42 CFR Part 2. HHS states that compliance with the 2024 Part 2 changes was required by 16 February 2026. Use current guidance, including restrictions concerning legal proceedings, rather than treating ordinary treatment sharing as permission for every disclosure.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the organisation, service and applicable state and federal rights or privacy duties. Arrange disability access, interpretation and culturally responsive participation. Check the legal basis for disclosure and whether specially protected records or proceedings are involved. Explain access, correction, complaints and any applicable patient-rights or legal review route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: HHS Office for Civil Rights handles covered HIPAA and Part 2 complaints; California and professional complaint routes address other matters. A subpoena, a court order and a routine agency request need distinct analysis. Seek appropriate advice rather than automatically releasing a complete file.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming HIPAA applies to every record or that a general consent covers all uses in legal proceedings.

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.
Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.
A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.
Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.
Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An associate is asked to provide unsupervised clinical services because a manager believes the social-work degree is sufficient.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the registration and supervision rules for the setting and arrange a compliant service. Explain the practitioner’s status accurately and escalate any pressure to exceed scope. Keep urgent support within the role while ensuring the appropriate licensed oversight.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A recipient’s hours are reduced while their support needs have increased, and the family is told only to find a more efficient worker.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Obtain the assessment and Notice of Action, compare authorised tasks with current evidence and assist with the appropriate hearing request if wanted. Address immediate care gaps separately. Staffing difficulties should not obscure a dispute about the assessment itself.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A relative with financial power of attorney signs for treatment while the patient’s healthcare directive names a different agent.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the patient’s own capacity for the treatment, then the directive and the agent’s operative authority. The financial document does not settle healthcare consent. Resolve the discrepancy through the responsible clinical and legal process before treating the signature as valid authority.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A facility says a person on an assessment hold cannot object to any medication or restraint because they are already detained.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Identify the separate authority and safeguards for each intervention. Explain the person’s rights and connect them with the appropriate advocate or attorney. Review necessity and less restrictive options; the hold does not supply a universal treatment or restraint permission.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A team uses an old training sheet to exclude personal safety and necessary medical care from a grave-disability assessment.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the current section 5008 definition and DHCS SB 43 guidance. Record the evidence connecting the qualifying condition to the inability to meet the relevant needs, consider available support and preserve the person’s review rights. The expanded definition still requires an individual legal assessment.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker reports suspected financial abuse to a supervisor and assumes that an internal form satisfies the legal duty.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check section 15630 and the setting-specific reporting route, make the required external report and document timing and recipient. Address the adult’s access to money and essential support. Internal reporting can support compliance but does not replace it.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A child discloses abuse and a manager directs the worker to wait for internal approval before calling the receiving agency.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Apply the reporting threshold and act within the statutory procedure without allowing internal approval to delay the duty. Record the child’s words, the report and immediate safety actions. Avoid conducting a separate investigation to obtain proof before reporting.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — California
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A court-related request seeks a client’s substance-use treatment record, and a worker relies on a general treatment-sharing consent.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check whether Part 2 applies and what the request, consent and current law permit for proceedings. Consider California requirements separately and seek the necessary advice. Document the disclosure decision and limit any release to what is lawfully authorised.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The California Board of Behavioral Sciences (BBS) regulates Licensed Clinical Social Workers (LCSWs) and Associate Clinical Social Workers (ASWs). Licensure, associate registration, supervision and employer duties must be distinguished. Use the current BBS statutes, regulations and guidance for the practice setting.

An ASW is not an independently licensed LCSW. A supervisor must meet the relevant requirements, and an employment title does not confer county-designated mental-health detention authority. NASW ethical material may inform practice but does not replace California licensing law.

Local pathway:
Confirm licence or registration status, practice setting and required supervision.
Explain the practitioner’s role, confidentiality limits and the purpose of the service.
Identify any separate statutory designation needed for assessment, reporting or detention work.
Use supervision and continuing education to address competence, bias and the person’s feedback.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
BBS investigates relevant professional complaints; county services, benefit agencies and courts address other decisions. Explain which route can address the person’s concern rather than presenting professional discipline as a service appeal.

Sources:
https://www.bbs.ca.gov/about/board_info.html
https://bbs.ca.gov/applicants/lcsw.html
https://www.bbs.ca.gov/about/law_reg.html

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) provides assessed in-home assistance to eligible aged, blind or disabled people. County assessment, authorised tasks and hours, financial or programme eligibility and actual provider arrangements are separate decisions. Medi-Cal services, regional-centre support and housing assistance have other rules.

An IHSS Notice of Action explains the county decision and hearing rights. A disagreement about authorised hours is different from a problem recruiting a worker or a complaint about missed visits. Identify the disputed decision and the evidence relevant to it.

Local pathway:
Apply through the appropriate county and identify the current eligibility and health-certification requirements.
Describe functional needs, actual assistance required and the home environment during assessment.
Check the authorised tasks, hours, notice and how a provider will be arranged.
Track the hearing or review route and any request concerning continued benefits while a decision is challenged.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
CDSS State Hearings handles relevant disputes, including IHSS decisions. Read the notice for the applicable deadline and any earlier action needed to seek continued assistance. A provider complaint does not automatically preserve a benefit-hearing deadline.

Sources:
https://www.cdss.ca.gov/in-home-supportive-services
https://www.cdss.ca.gov/hearing-requests
https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/home-and-community-based-services-hcbs-grievance-and-hearings/

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
California’s Probate Code provides decision-specific capacity and healthcare decision-making provisions, including advance healthcare directives, agents and surrogate arrangements. Probate conservatorship and Lanterman-Petris-Short (LPS) conservatorship are different processes; neither should be described simply as a family member taking over all decisions.

Read the directive, power or court order and identify the exact authority. Financial power does not automatically include healthcare. Where no existing authorised decision-maker is available, use the applicable Probate Code surrogate process with the responsible healthcare provider rather than assuming an informal next-of-kin hierarchy.

Local pathway:
Identify the specific healthcare, personal or financial decision and support the person’s participation.
Check the relevant capacity standard and evidence rather than relying on diagnosis alone.
Read the advance directive, appointment or court order and verify scope and operation.
Use the applicable surrogate or court route if authority is missing or disputed.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
California Courts explains advance planning and conservatorship routes. A clinical consent dispute and a conservatorship petition have different procedures. Seek the relevant legal or clinical advice and preserve the person’s wishes and participation.

Sources:
https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/wills-estates-probate/legal-documents
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4712.
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=810.

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The LPS framework provides particular mental-health detention and conservatorship routes. Probate conservatorship, healthcare consent and facility restraint rules are separate. An admission agreement or conservator’s general status does not explain every locked-door measure, restraint or treatment.

A section 5150 hold is a time-limited assessment and crisis-intervention route, not an automatic order to keep someone for the whole maximum period or to impose every proposed treatment. Continuing detention requires the applicable further authority and safeguards.

Local pathway:
Identify the actual restriction, setting and the legal measure relied on.
Read the hold, court order or specific restraint authority and check its scope and expiry.
Distinguish the person’s detention status from medication consent and other healthcare decisions.
Arrange patients’ rights support, the appropriate hearing or court route and a plan to reduce restrictions.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
County patients’ rights advocates and legal representatives help with applicable detention and treatment rights. Certification review and medication-capacity hearings address different questions. Explain the route relevant to the person’s objection rather than describing every challenge as the same appeal.

Sources:
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=5150.
https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/patients-rights/
https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/DHCS_Handbook_English.pdf

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Lanterman-Petris-Short framework in the Welfare and Institutions Code includes section 5150 assessment and crisis intervention, subsequent certification routes and conservatorship. Section 5150 permits specified authorised persons to act on probable cause under the statutory conditions, for up to 72 hours. It is not a power held by every social worker.

SB 43 expanded the grave-disability definition to include specified circumstances involving severe substance use disorder and inability to meet needs including personal safety or necessary medical care. Counties could defer implementation only until January 2026. Use the current section 5008 wording and criteria rather than an older food-clothing-shelter-only summary.

Local pathway:
Identify the authorised person, proposed route and evidence for the current statutory criteria.
Consider voluntary crisis support and whether the person can be served without detention.
Check the start time, required assessment, notices and any further certification or court process.
Keep detention and treatment-consent safeguards separate, including medication-capacity procedures where applicable.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain access to the patients’ rights advocate, legal representation and the relevant hearing or court review. Additional detention is not automatic when an initial period ends. A broad social problem or lack of housing should not be substituted for the required statutory analysis.

Sources:
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=5150.
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=5008.
https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/SB-43-FAQs.pdf

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
California’s Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act includes mandated-reporting duties. Welfare and Institutions Code section 15630 addresses covered reporters and circumstances. County APS service eligibility and the statutory definitions used for reporting should be checked separately; an agency’s service age range should not be substituted for the legal definition.

Community, long-term-care, state-hospital and other institutional concerns can have different reporting recipients and timing rules. CDSS publishes general reporting guidance, but the actual setting and allegation determine which statutory provisions apply.

Local pathway:
Identify the person’s statutory category, your reporting role, the alleged harm and the setting.
Make the required report through the correct APS, law-enforcement, ombudsman or other specified route.
Check the applicable telephone and written or electronic follow-up deadlines; do not assume one rule covers every institution.
Arrange immediate safety, consent-sensitive support and follow-up while preserving the adult’s account.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A mandated report and the adult’s consent to ongoing services are different matters. Reporting does not itself appoint a conservator or authorise forced placement. Explain the relevant APS, regulatory, police or court process and available advocacy.

Sources:
https://www.cdss.ca.gov/inforesources/cdss-programs/adult-protective-services/information-for-mandated-reporters
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=15630.
https://cdss.ca.gov/adult-protective-services

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act (CANRA) specifies mandated reporters, reportable concerns and recipients. Penal Code section 11166 requires a covered reporter acting professionally or within employment to report knowledge or reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect. Certainty or medical proof is not required.

The ordinary procedure requires an initial telephone report immediately or as soon as practicably possible and a written follow-up within 36 hours. Reporting to a supervisor is not a substitute. Use the current statutory recipient and procedure, including any applicable special circumstances.

Local pathway:
Identify your mandated-reporter role and the facts supporting knowledge or reasonable suspicion.
Make the required report to an authorised receiving agency and address immediate danger.
Complete the follow-up within the applicable time and record what was reported.
Coordinate support and assess any dependency-court or Indian Child Welfare Act requirements where relevant.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain confidentiality limits and the child’s and family’s access to support or legal advice. A mandated report does not itself establish the legal grounds for removal or a court finding. Preserve the distinction between suspicion, investigation and adjudication.

Sources:
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=11166.
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=11165.7.

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
California practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Federal disability and civil-rights requirements and California protections apply according to the service and decision. For confidentiality, distinguish HIPAA-covered entities, California’s Confidentiality of Medical Information Act and other applicable state rules. A social-work record is not automatically governed by HIPAA solely because it contains sensitive information.

Certain substance-use-disorder records have additional protection under 42 CFR Part 2. HHS states that compliance with the 2024 Part 2 changes was required by 16 February 2026. Use current guidance, including restrictions concerning legal proceedings, rather than treating ordinary treatment sharing as permission for every disclosure.

Local pathway:
Identify the organisation, service and applicable state and federal rights or privacy duties.
Arrange disability access, interpretation and culturally responsive participation.
Check the legal basis for disclosure and whether specially protected records or proceedings are involved.
Explain access, correction, complaints and any applicable patient-rights or legal review route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
HHS Office for Civil Rights handles covered HIPAA and Part 2 complaints; California and professional complaint routes address other matters. A subpoena, a court order and a routine agency request need distinct analysis. Seek appropriate advice rather than automatically releasing a complete file.

Sources:
https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/mental-health/index.html
https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/part-2/index.html
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.10.
